newsitem.title: INDIA: Parliament panel urges India to build Agni missile.
newsitem.headline: Parliament panel urges India to build Agni missile.

text.p: An Indian parliamentary panel on Wednesday urged New Delhi to press on with building a controversial intermediate-range missile to counter potential threats from neighbouring China and Pakistan.
"India has no option but to continue to develop and upgrade its missile capabilities for deterrence against any adventurist intentions of a hostile country," the panel said in a report.
The panel's recommendations are not binding.

"The committee reiterates...that the government should review their Technology Demonstrator-Agni Missile Project to take it to its logical conclusion where it can contribute to the defence and deterrence capabilities of the country," it said.
India last December said it had completed research on the Agni missile, but had no plans to produce the 14-tonne, 19-metre (60-foot) rocket.
The 2,500-km (1,500-mile) range Agni is believed capable of carrying a nuclear warhead and is seen as a potential deterrent to China.
China and India fought a brief border war in 1962. Indian analysts say China's first nuclear test two years later prompted India's only nuclear test in 1974.
Pakistan and India, who have gone to war three times since 1947, say they have no nuclear arms but experts say either can assemble them swiftly.

Pakistan and China have denied Western reports that Beijing transferred to Islamabad nuclear weapons components and Chinese M-11 missiles that can deliver nuclear warheads. But India views their close ties with concern.
The Defence Ministry's annual report released earlier this month said India was pressing ahead with other missile development programmes, but remained silent on the Agni.
The United States and other countries have opposed India's missile programme, which Washington says could upset regional stability.

Referring to China and Pakistan, the parliamentary committee report said: "With both these countries we have unsettled boundary disputes and hence there is the need for greater attention to this aspect of our defence preparedness."
"Capabilities of a country take a long time to build up while the intentions of countries can change overnight," it added.
